questions.question: In DFS of an UNDIRECTED graph, can you ever find a 'forward edge'?
questions.solutionApproach: No — in undirected graphs, DFS only ever produces tree edges and back edges. Forward and cross edges cannot occur because of how undirected traversal discovers neighbors symmetrically.
questions.answer: No — undirected graph DFS only has tree and back edges.

questions.question: Does a DFS tree give the shortest path (in edges) from the source to every other vertex, same as BFS?
questions.solutionApproach: No — only BFS guarantees this. DFS can produce arbitrarily long paths to a vertex even if a much shorter path exists, since DFS goes deep before backtracking rather than exploring level by level.
questions.answer: No — this guarantee is specific to BFS, not DFS.

A sparse graph has V=1000 vertices and E=2000 edges, represented as an adjacency matrix. What is the DFS time complexity?
questions.solutionApproach: Adjacency matrix forces O(V²) regardless of actual edge count, since checking all possible neighbors of each vertex costs O(V) each. O(V²) = O(1,000,000), even though E is much smaller.
questions.answer: O(V²) = O(1,000,000) — adjacency matrix representation ignores edge sparsity.
